analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage in steps from $4.25 to $5.30 an hour by 2000.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in a House subcommittee until the Congress ended, with 6 cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act to raise the federal minimum wage from $4.25 an hour to $4.60 in 1996, then in yearly steps to $5.30 starting in 2000 [S2][S3]. It was introduced in February 1995, referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities, and sent to its Workforce Protections subcommittee two weeks later [S5]. No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed, and the bill died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997 [S5]. A different minimum wage bill did pass in 1996, raising the wage to $4.75 and then $5.15.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers paid at or near the federal minimum — roughly $4.25 an hour at the time — would see their pay rise in five annual steps to $5.30 by 2000, about a 25% increase [S3].

how_it_helps.text: Raises the minimum wage in five annual steps: $4.60 in 1996, $4.85 in 1997, $5.00 in 1998, $5.15 in 1999, and $5.30 from 2000 onward, replacing the $4.25 floor [S2][S3].
The phased schedule spreads the increase over five years, giving employers time to adjust rather than imposing a sudden jump [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers of low-wage workers — concentrated in fast food, restaurants, retail, and agriculture — would bear higher payroll costs, and some of that cost could be passed on through prices or absorbed through reduced hours [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Restaurants, retail, and other low-wage employers

drawbacks.text: A roughly 25% increase in the wage floor over five years would raise labor costs for businesses that employ many minimum-wage workers, particularly small restaurants and retailers [S3].

Opponents of minimum wage increases generally argue that a higher wage floor prices some entry-level and low-skill workers out of jobs or reduces hours; that trade-off was never tested in hearings or debate because the bill got none.

The bill was a simple wage schedule with no offsetting small-business relief (such as the tip-credit or training-wage provisions that accompanied the 1996 increase), which likely made it harder to move [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A higher wage floor directly raises pay for the lowest-earning workers, a real and easily understood gain. The cost falls on a diffuse set of employers and partly on consumers through prices, and the strongest honest objection is possible job or hour losses at the bottom of the wage ladder. The five-year phase-in blunts both sides. In the event, Congress passed a similar-but-smaller increase in 1996 ($4.75, then $5.15), so the practical gap between this bill and the law that followed was modest.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the House education and labor committee, and two weeks later sent to a subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. James Clyburn introduced the Liveable Wage Act on February 1, 1995 [S1][S5].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities on the day of introduction [S5].
On February 17, 1995, it was referred to the subcommittee on Workforce Protections — the last action ever recorded on the bill [S4] no, [S5].
The bill attracted 6 cosponsors (5 Democrats and 1 Independent) and never advanced further before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997 [S4].
Separately, in 1996 Congress did enact a minimum wage increase to $4.75 in 1996 and $5.15 in 1997 as part of another bill, so a substantial share of what this bill sought happened by other means.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Low-wage employers benefited from another two years at the $4.25 floor before the 1996 law took effect, though minimum-wage workers ended up with most of the increase anyway through the separate 1996 law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Low-wage employers, until the 1996 law passed

for.name: Rep. James E. Clyburn
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Liveable Wage Act of 1995 and delivered introductory remarks on the House floor

against.name: Rep. William Goodling
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities
against.what_they_did: Committee never advanced the bill past its subcommittee referral; no markup or floor consideration occurred during the 104th Congress

sides.party_line_note: No committee or floor vote was ever recorded, so the partisan split cannot be measured; the bill died in a committee controlled by the new Republican majority with only Democratic and Independent cosponsors [S4][S5].

industries.note: Restaurants employ the largest share of minimum-wage workers and would have absorbed the biggest payroll increase under the bill's five-step schedule. Its interest in the bill's failure ran against the pay of the lowest-wage workers.

industries.industry: Retail and other low-wage service employers
industries.note: Retail, agriculture, and similar sectors pay many workers near the minimum and would have faced phased payroll increases to $5.30 by 2000. The bill's death kept their labor costs unchanged for two more years.
